newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian refugees condemn violence, intimidation.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian refugees condemn violence, intimidation.

text.p: Moslem, Croat and Serb refugees joined forces on Wednesday to condemn a rising tide of ethnic violence in Bosnia aimed at preventing people from returning to their pre-war homes.

"We reject ideologies of ethnic separation and demand the full implementation of the peace agreement for Bosnia-Herzegovina," said a statement issued by associations of displaced persons and refugees from across Bosnia.
Members of refugee associations from at least 17 towns said they planned to form a coalition to resist attempts by nationalist authorities to keep the country divided into ethnically "pure" areas.
"We all want to return to our homes and believe that we can only achieve this goal through solidarity with one another and by acting together," the statement said.
The international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, supported the refugees' initiative, Michael Steiner, Bildt's deputy, said.
Steiner praised the founding of the "Coalition for Return" as a crucial step in fighting authorities intent on sealing the results of ethnic cleansing and conquest.
"The burning issue of (refugee) return is not just something which is of concern of one ethnicity," Steiner told a news conference in Sarajevo.
Steiner held talks with the refugee leaders after a series of bombing and arson attacks hit Bosnia this month.
More than 90 Moslem houses and two mosques were destroyed in several abandoned villages near Serb-held Prijedor in the course of several hours last week.
The NATO-led peace force said the demolition around Prijedor appeared systematic. Several 10 kg (20 pound) anti-tank mines were rigged to each house.
In Croat-held Drvar to the south, 65 Serb houses in two villages were torched over several days.
On Tuesday night, two explosions damaged houses in a Serb-controlled area recently resettled by Moslem refugees, U.N. officials said earlier.
The recent escalation in violence "has been calculated to increase the atmosphere of fear and intimidation that prevents the return of displaced and refugees to their homes," the statement said.
Steiner acknowledged that the refugees faced a difficult fight against powerful forces in Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat territories who oppose refugees returning to their homes.
"We have no illusions about how difficult this job is," he said.

The U.S.-brokered peace accord signed last December guarantees refugees the right to return to their homes. But nationalist authorities across Bosnia have blocked attempts by people to move back and have moved in their own refugees into abandoned homes.
